tutor.name: Tutor
tutor.fallback: I’m a scripted demo tutor, so I only know this problem. Try “hint”, “why”, or ask about a word in the step.
tutor.noSpoil: I’d rather not hand you the answer: you’ll keep it longer if you find it. Here’s a nudge instead.
tutor.hintsOut: That was my last hint for this part. Read the step out loud, slowly; the slip is usually where a word and a symbol disagree.

scenarios.subject: physics
scenarios.title: Forces on a block on an incline
scenarios.problem: A 2.0 kg block slides down a 30° incline. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.20. Find the block’s acceleration. Take g = 9.8 m/s².
intro: Hi Priya. A classmate worked this one and got a ≈ 2.9 m/s², but the key says 3.2 m/s². Somewhere in their five steps, one line went wrong. We’ll find it together.
First, the problem itself. Read it on the sheet: what is it actually asking for?

read.question: What does the problem ask for?
options: The block’s acceleration down the slope
The normal force on the block
The coefficient of friction
read.right: Yes: one number, the acceleration along the slope. Everything else (normal force, friction) is a stepping stone to it.
read.wrong: Not quite. That shows up along the way, but look at the last sentence of the problem: “Find the block’s …”

scenarios.check: Now the classmate’s working. I’ll lay each step on the desk. Tell me if it holds up, or if something’s off.

steps.text: Forces on the block: weight mg straight down, normal force N perpendicular to the slope, kinetic friction f up the slope.
steps.say: Step 1 is the free-body diagram. I’ve lit the three forces on the sketch. Does this list look right to you?
steps.ok: Agreed. The block slides down, so friction points up the slope, against the motion.
steps.nudge: This one actually holds up: three forces, and friction opposes the sliding, so up the slope is right. Keep it in mind as we go.

steps.text: Along the slope, gravity pulls with mg sin 30° = 19.6 × 0.5 = 9.8 N.
steps.say: Step 2 takes the part of the weight that runs along the slope. Check the trig and the arithmetic.
steps.ok: Right. The along-slope part uses sin θ, and 19.6 × 0.5 is 9.8 N.
steps.nudge: Look again: sin 30° is exactly 0.5, and the along-slope part of the weight is mg sin θ. This step is fine.

steps.text: The normal force balances the weight: N = mg = 2.0 × 9.8 = 19.6 N.
steps.say: Step 3 finds the normal force. This is the one the friction depends on, so look carefully.
steps.missed: Hmm, look again. On a flat floor N = mg. But this floor is tilted 30°. Does the surface push back against the whole weight, or only part of it?
steps.caught: Good catch. That’s the slip: N = mg is only true on a flat surface.

why.question: Why is N = mg wrong here?
options: On a slope the surface only pushes back against mg cos θ, the part of the weight pressing into it
The normal force should be mg sin θ
The normal force should include friction
why.right: Exactly. The weight splits in two: mg cos θ presses into the slope, and mg sin θ pulls along it. The surface only answers the first.
why.wrong: Not that one. Look at the sketch: which dashed part of the weight points straight into the slope?

fix.question: So what should step 3 say?
options: N = mg sin 30° = 9.8 N
N = mg + f
fix.right: That’s the line. I’ll fix the card, and then the rest of the solution follows from your number.
fix.wrong: Close, but that’s the along-slope part. We want the part perpendicular to the slope.

after.say: With your N, friction drops to about 3.4 N. The classmate’s 3.92 N came from the wrong N.

after.text: Net force along the slope: ma = 9.8 − 3.4 = 6.4 N, so a = 6.4 ÷ 2.0 ≈ 3.2 m/s².
after.say: Pull minus friction, divided by mass: 3.2 m/s². That matches the key.

scenarios.rule: On a slope, N = mg cos θ, not mg. Check N first: friction inherits any error in it.

read: The last sentence of a problem usually names the unknown.
check: One step uses a rule that’s true on flat ground but not on a slope.
Compare each force with the sketch: does the surface push back against all of the weight?
Look at step 3: does N really equal mg on a 30° slope?
fix: The part of the weight pressing into the slope uses cos θ.

faq.reply: The angle between the weight and the line perpendicular to the slope equals the incline angle θ. So the perpendicular part is mg cos θ and the along-slope part is mg sin θ.
Kinetic friction is f = μN. It always uses the normal force, which is why an error in N spreads into friction and then into the acceleration.
“Normal” means perpendicular. The normal force is the surface pushing straight out of itself, against whatever presses into it.

scenarios.subject: chemistry
scenarios.title: Grams to moles to grams
scenarios.problem: Hydrogen burns in oxygen: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. How many grams of water form when 8.0 g of O₂ reacts completely? Use O₂ = 32.00 g/mol and H₂O = 18.02 g/mol.
intro: Hi Priya. A classmate got 0.028 g of water from this reaction; the key says 9.0 g. That’s a big gap, so one step must have flipped something. Let’s find it.
Start with the sheet. What quantity is the problem after?

read.question: What does the problem ask for?
options: The mass of water produced
The moles of oxygen used
The mass of hydrogen needed
read.right: Right: grams of water. So the chain has to start in grams of O₂ and end in grams of H₂O. I’ve lit that path on the sheet.
read.wrong: That’s a stop along the way. Read the question again: “How many grams of …”

scenarios.check: Here’s the classmate’s chain, one step at a time. Watch the units at each step: they’re the best lie detector in chemistry.

steps.text: Moles of O₂: 8.0 g ÷ 32.00 g/mol = 0.25 mol.
steps.say: Step 1 turns grams of O₂ into moles. Divide by molar mass: do the units cancel to mol?
steps.ok: Yes. g ÷ (g/mol) leaves mol, and they used O₂ = 32.00, not O = 16.00. Nice.
steps.nudge: This one’s sound: 8.0 ÷ 32.00 = 0.25, and grams divided by grams-per-mole leaves moles.

steps.text: Mole ratio from the equation: 0.25 mol O₂ × (2 mol H₂O ÷ 1 mol O₂) = 0.50 mol H₂O.
steps.say: Step 2 crosses the equation with the mole ratio. Check the coefficients: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O.
steps.ok: Right. One O₂ makes two H₂O, so the moles double.
steps.nudge: Look again: the equation has 1 O₂ and 2 H₂O, so 0.25 mol of O₂ really does make 0.50 mol of water. This step holds.

steps.text: Mass of water: 0.50 mol ÷ 18.02 g/mol ≈ 0.028 g.
steps.say: Step 3 turns moles of water back into grams. Track the units here.
steps.missed: Let’s check the units together: mol ÷ (g/mol) = mol²/g. Is that a mass?
steps.caught: Exactly. Dividing by molar mass goes from grams to moles. Going back to grams, you multiply.

why.question: What went wrong in step 3?
options: It divided by molar mass; to get grams from moles you multiply, and the units show it
It should have used the molar mass of O₂
The mole ratio is upside down
why.right: Yes. mol × (g/mol) = g. The units would have caught it: their answer was in mol²/g.
why.wrong: Not quite. Steps 1 and 2 checked out. Look only at the last arrow on the sketch and its units.

fix.question: What should step 3 say?
fix.right: That’s it. I’ll fix the card and the arrow on the sketch.
fix.wrong: Check which amount of water you have (step 2) and which way the units need to go.

scenarios.fixed: Mass of water: 0.50 mol × 18.02 g/mol ≈ 9.0 g.

after.text: Check by conservation of mass: 0.50 mol H₂ × 2.016 g/mol ≈ 1.0 g of H₂ reacts, and 8.0 g + 1.0 g = 9.0 g. It balances.
after.say: A quick sanity check: the mass going in must equal the mass coming out. 9.0 g in, 9.0 g out.

scenarios.rule: Grams → moles: divide by molar mass. Moles → grams: multiply. If the units don’t end in grams, the step is wrong.

read: Look for the unit in the question: “how many grams of …”
The unknown is a mass of water.
check: Write the units next to every number.
One step ends in mol²/g, which isn’t a mass.
Look at step 3: should you divide or multiply by g/mol to get grams?
fix: Use the 0.50 mol of water from step 2.

faq.reply: Molar mass is grams per mole. Divide grams by it to get moles; multiply moles by it to get grams.
The coefficients in the balanced equation are mole ratios: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O means 1 mol O₂ makes 2 mol H₂O.
Carry units through every step, like numbers. If they don’t cancel down to the unit you want, the step is wrong.

scenarios.subject: biology
scenarios.title: From DNA to protein
scenarios.problem: A DNA template strand reads 3′-TAC AAG CCT ATT GCA-5′. Write the amino acid sequence of the protein it codes for.
scenarios._derivation: Template 3'-TAC AAG CCT ATT GCA-5' -> mRNA 5'-AUG UUC GGA UAA CGU-3'. AUG Met, UUC Phe, GGA Gly, UAA stop. CGU (Arg) is after the stop and is not translated.
intro: Hi Priya. A classmate turned this DNA into Met–Phe–Gly–Arg, but the key stops at Met–Phe–Gly. One amino acid too many. Let’s see where it crept in.
I’ll scaffold the first part with you. On the sheet: what form should the answer take?

read.question: What does the problem ask for?
options: The amino acid sequence of the protein
The mRNA sequence
The coding DNA strand
read.right: Right: amino acids. The mRNA is a step on the way there. DNA → mRNA → protein, left to right on the sketch.
read.wrong: That’s a middle step. The last word of the question tells you the final form: “the protein it codes for”.

scenarios.check: Here are the classmate’s steps. Use the sketch: each column is one codon, read top to bottom.

steps.text: Transcribe: pair each template base, A→U, T→A, C→G, G→C. mRNA: 5′-AUG UUC GGA UAA CGU-3′.
steps.say: Step 1 builds the mRNA from the template. Check a codon or two against the pairing rules.
steps.ok: Correct. TAC pairs to AUG, and so on. RNA uses U in place of T.
steps.nudge: This one’s right: T pairs with A, A with U (RNA has no T), C with G. TAC → AUG checks out.

steps.text: Start at the start codon AUG: Met. Then UUC → Phe, GGA → Gly.
steps.say: Step 2 starts translating. AUG is the start codon. Check the next two in the codon table.
steps.ok: Yes. Start at AUG, then read three bases at a time: UUC Phe, GGA Gly.
steps.nudge: Look again: AUG is Met (and the start signal), UUC is Phe, GGA is Gly. This one holds up.

steps.text: Next, UAA has no amino acid, so skip it and read on: CGU → Arg. Protein: Met–Phe–Gly–Arg.
steps.say: Step 3 deals with the last two codons. What does UAA tell the ribosome?
steps.missed: Look at UAA again. “No amino acid” is true, but is it a gap to skip, or a signal?
steps.caught: That’s the one. UAA isn’t a gap, it’s a stop signal.

why.question: Why is step 3 wrong?
options: UAA is a stop codon: the ribosome lets go, so nothing after it is translated
UAA codes for leucine
The reading frame shifted by one base
why.right: Yes. A stop codon ends translation. CGU is still in the mRNA, but it’s never read.
why.wrong: Not quite. The pairing and the frame were fine in steps 1 and 2. Focus on what UAA means.

fix.question: What should step 3 say?
options: UAA is a stop codon, so translation ends. Protein: Met–Phe–Gly
Skip UAA and read on. Protein: Met–Phe–Gly–Arg
UAA codes for Tyr. Protein: Met–Phe–Gly–Tyr–Arg
fix.right: That’s the fix. I’ll update the card and mark the stop on the sketch.
fix.wrong: Remember what a stop codon does to the ribosome.

scenarios.fixed: UAA is a stop codon, so translation ends. Protein: Met–Phe–Gly.

after.text: Check: three codons before the stop give three amino acids. The stop codon itself codes for none.
after.say: Count check: three codons before the stop, three amino acids. The key agrees.

scenarios.rule: Translation runs from AUG to the first stop codon (UAA, UAG or UGA). Nothing after the stop is read.

read: Read the last few words of the question.
“The protein it codes for” means amino acids.
check: Not every codon codes for an amino acid.
Three codons don’t code for any amino acid. What do they do instead?
Look at step 3: is UAA something to skip, or a stop?
fix: The ribosome releases the chain at a stop codon.
Only the codons before UAA are translated.

faq.reply: UAA, UAG and UGA are stop codons. A release factor binds there and the finished chain is let go.
The template strand is the one RNA polymerase reads. The mRNA is complementary to it, so it matches the coding strand (with U for T).
AUG is the start codon and codes for methionine (Met), so most proteins begin with Met.
